title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
text: Teaching · UC San Diego · Spring 2022 and 2023 · SE 168/268

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
text:
One Structure, Three Connected Stages
The course followed a bolted cantilever plate throughout. Students first predicted its vibration, then measured it, and finally reconciled the model with the test. This made the purpose of each exercise concrete: a sensor location, sampling choice, or boundary assumption could affect the final correlation.


Pre-Test — predict modes, select measurement locations, and plan the test.
Test — apply a measured force, record responses, and check the data.
Post-Test — identify modes, correlate the model, and investigate a structural change.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
section: Planning a Test the Model Can Explain
text:
Planning a Test the Model Can Explain
The early labs built mass, stiffness, and damping models, then moved to a finite-element model of the plate. Target modes and their shapes guided the choice of measurement locations. Guyan reduction connected the many model degrees of freedom to the smaller set available for measurement.
That preparation came into the lab. The target frequency band guided the sampling rate, hammer-tip selection, and excitation settings; the decay time helped set the record length. Channel locations, measurement directions, and units had to agree with the model.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
text:
Leading the Vibration Tests
I led the experiment sessions around two ways of exciting the same plate. For impact testing, I guided students through hammer-tip selection, a clean single hit, and repeated measurements. A double hit or an overloaded channel needed attention while the setup was still available.
For shaker testing, I guided band-limited random excitation and the acquisition setup. The load cell measured the applied force, while accelerometers measured the response. Comparing hammer and shaker measurements helped students connect excitation bandwidth, repeatability, and signal quality to the frequency range they wanted to identify.



The instrumented hammer provides a short force input; the shaker supplies controlled excitation over a selected band. Equipment photographs from the course seDAQ hardware guide, pages 9 and 11.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
section: Checking Data Before Leaving the Lab
text:
Checking Data Before Leaving the Lab
I emphasized checking channel definitions, sensitivity settings, polarity, and signal levels before accepting a record. We inspected time histories for double hits, clipping, and incomplete decay, then checked whether the force spectrum covered the target modes.
Frequency response functions (FRFs) relate measured acceleration to applied force. Coherence and reciprocity provided further checks on the measurements and channel definitions. A weak response or poor coherence prompted investigation of the excitation, sensor location, and processing choices.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
text:
Turning Measurements into Modes
The post-test labs used MATLAB to estimate auto- and cross-spectra, FRFs, and coherence, with averaging and windowing suited to the excitation. Students compared impact and shaker results before choosing the data for modal identification.
In IMAT/OPoly, they extracted natural frequencies, damping, and mode shapes, checked stable poles, and compared reconstructed FRFs with the measurements. The sequence separated the quality of the recorded data from the quality of the fitted modal model.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
section: Correlating the Model and Identifying a Change
text:
Correlating the Model and Identifying a Change
The final stage compared test and model frequencies, mode shapes, and FRFs. Mode matching, modal assurance, and cross-orthogonality helped establish which modes could be compared. Model updating then adjusted uncertain plate and boundary stiffnesses, rather than assuming the bolted edge was perfectly fixed.




Test and analysis must describe the same coordinates and units before their modes and FRFs are compared. Updating revises uncertain physical parameters, and a new measurement set tests the resulting model. Original summary of the course’s correlation sequence.



The final project introduced an added spring at an unknown location. Students used a new measurement set and their correlated baseline model to estimate its location and stiffness, then explain their reasoning across the full test-and-analysis process.

title: Structural Vibration Testing and Model Correlation
text:
What It Means
My main contribution was making the experimental stage work: connecting instrumentation and excitation choices to trustworthy measurements, then helping students use those measurements in a dynamic model. These experimental modal-analysis skills carry across structural, mechanical, and aerospace testing: plan the test, troubleshoot at the bench, and explain the agreement or discrepancy with analysis.

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
text: Doctoral Research · UC San Diego · 2021–2023 · USACE/ERDC

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
section: A Corrosion Model That Feels Stress
text:
A Corrosion Model That Feels Stress
Most corrosion models used in practice are empirical curves fitted to past data, which rarely exist for gates like these. I built one on the physics instead.
The phase-field model couples four sets of equations: the electrochemical reaction at the metal surface, the transport of dissolved ions, the electric potential, and mechanical equilibrium. Because stress enters the reaction kinetics, the model can tell tension from compression, which many earlier phase-field models did not capture.
The results matched physical intuition. Tension makes pits deeper and sharper, compression flattens them, and shear tilts their growth. Cyclic loading also produced crack-like tails in some simulations.



The same pit grows differently under tension, no load, and compression, shown with the hydrostatic stress around it. Source: Scientific Reports 2022.

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
text:
Stress-Based Crack Initiation
As a pit deepens and sharpens, stress concentrates at its tip. I used the pit depth and tip curvature to estimate this concentration, then proposed a crack-initiation criterion based on whether the local stress reaches the von Mises yield limit.




The same pit is shown as morphology (left) and a stress field (right), with both domains at the same scale. Stress concentrates at the sharpened tip. This local concentration drives the crack-initiation check. Source: doctoral defense presentation, slide 57.



I compared this stress-based criterion with the Tsujikawa–Kondo criterion, which compares crack and pit growth rates. In the simulated example, the stress-based criterion gives an earlier, more stable initiation prediction: its stress history rises smoothly, while the growth-rate indicator fluctuates.




The stress-based criterion (red, left axis) reaches its 410 MPa threshold before the growth-rate criterion (blue, right axis) reaches its threshold of Kv = 2. Insets show the pit at the two predicted initiation points. Source: dissertation, Fig. 2.5; doctoral defense, slide 58.

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
text:
A 40-Minute Simulation in Seconds
A physics model this detailed is slow: each run took over 40 minutes. Risk analysis needs thousands of runs, so I built a surrogate.
From 255 simulations, a convolutional autoencoder learned to describe each 80 × 40 corrosion image with just six numbers, where principal component analysis would need hundreds.
I then trained Gaussian-process nonlinear autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (GP-NARX) to forecast those six features. Each prediction uses the previous five time steps together with the applied stress and corrosion parameters. Feeding predictions back into the model gives a longer forecast, with uncertainty, which the decoder turns back into corrosion images.




The CNN encoder maps a corrosion image into six features. GP-NARX forecasts those features recursively from their recent history and the physical inputs; the decoder reconstructs future pit shapes. Source: dissertation, Fig. 3.1; doctoral defense, slide 35.







Each row shows a later time: the original simulation, the mean forecast and its error, then the decoded Gaussian-process mean and its error. Source: doctoral defense, slide 46; Scientific Reports 2022.

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
text:
Keeping the Surrogate Physical
To keep long forecasts consistent with continuing material loss, I contributed my phase-field simulations and baseline surrogate to a physics-constrained version. Its loss function penalizes predictions in which corroded material reappears.
The extension reduced mean squared error from 0.0125 to 0.0066. In the published benchmark, forecasting 200 time steps took 1.3 seconds with the extension and 5.4 seconds with the original surrogate, after training.




The physics loss constrains material loss while the encoder and decoder compress and reconstruct pit shapes. Source: MSSP 2023, 110515.

title: Multiphysics Corrosion Simulation and Surrogate Modeling
text:
What It Means
The phase-field model explains how load shapes corrosion, and the surrogate makes that physics fast enough to run thousands of times. That speed is what made the next step possible: carrying uncertainty through the model to a risk map of an entire gate. Later, I mentored Haiwei Lin in extending the model from crack initiation to crack growth.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
text: Doctoral and Postdoctoral Research · UC San Diego with Cal Poly · 2022–2025

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
text:
Updating from Synthetic Corrosion Images
I first developed and tested the image-based methods using synthetic inspection images rendered in Blender from simulated corrosion. Their known model parameters provided a reference for checking the inference. The observations used for updating were the pit counts and opening sizes extracted from those images.
A U-Net finds the pits, and super-resolution and circle detection measure their openings. A two-stage method called approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) updates the model: pit counts inform how pits start, and opening widths inform how fast they grow. Once updated, the physics predicts pit depth, which the camera cannot see.




A U-Net segments pits in a Blender-rendered inspection image; thresholding then defines their openings. Source: doctoral defense presentation, slide 74.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
section: Faster Inference for the Image Study
text:
Faster Inference for the Image Study
ABC found parameters by rerunning the model again and again, which took hours. I replaced that search with two trained networks: a summary network that condenses the observations, and a conditional invertible neural network that turns them directly into plausible parameter values.
In this synthetic-image benchmark, about five hours of training reduced each update from four hours to four seconds. Posterior standard deviations were roughly four to seven times smaller than with ABC. That speed makes repeated updating practical.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
text:
Updating from Real Laser Scans
I then worked with Duncan Fure and Long Wang at Cal Poly on real corrosion measurements. Stainless-steel specimens were corroded in ferric chloride at 50 °C for 15 minutes to 3 hours, then laser-scanned at 4 µm spacing in the surface plane. I extracted pit-opening radius distributions from these scans for model updating.



Real laser-scan depth maps at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 hours of exposure (a–e), with one pit enlarged (f). Color gives depth below the surface in millimeters. Source: IWSHM 2025 model-updating presentation, slide 9.


I updated a hybrid model of phase-field pit growth and probabilistic pit initiation using the first four exposure times. A summary network and conditional invertible neural network inferred parameter distributions from the measured pit-size distributions. The three-hour scans were reserved for checking the forecast.




Inference workflow for the real laser-scan study: the summary network condenses the observed pit-size distributions, and the inference network estimates model parameters. Green arrows show training; dashed red arrows show inference. Source: IWSHM 2025 model-updating presentation, slide 11.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
section: What the Measurements Tell the Model
text:
What the Measurements Tell the Model
The experimental observations concentrated the posterior distributions of the pit-initiation parameters λ and β and the reaction parameter θ₁. The diffusion parameter θ₂ remained broadly distributed, showing that these measurements constrain reaction kinetics more strongly than diffusion under the accelerated-test conditions.



Parameter distributions updated from the real laser-scan observations: priors in green, posteriors in red, and posterior means in black. Initiation and reaction parameters concentrate, while the diffusion parameter remains broad. Source: IWSHM 2025 model-updating presentation, slide 13; JCSHM manuscript, Fig. 10.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
text:
Forecasting the Pit-Size Distribution
I propagated these posterior parameter distributions through the model to forecast pit sizes at the held-out three-hour time point. The updated model predicted a 95th-percentile radius of 0.169 mm, against 0.190 mm measured and 0.286 mm from the power law: errors of −11% and +51%, respectively.
The mean pit count was also close: 760 predicted, against 804 observed.



Pit-opening radius percentiles over time. At the held-out three-hour point, model updating is closer to the measurements for the 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles. Source: IWSHM 2025 model-updating presentation, slide 15; JCSHM manuscript, Table 2.

title: Bayesian Model Updating with Real Measurements
text:
What It Means
The synthetic-image study established the observation-to-parameter workflow and made inference fast. The laser-scan study carried that workflow into real experiments, from measured pit sizes to posterior parameters and a later-time forecast. Together, they show how repeated observations can refine corrosion predictions.

  What I DoThree Questions Behind My Work
  Across these projects, in research and in practice, the work comes back to the same three questions.
  
    01 · MonitorHow Is the Structure Behaving?Reading a structure's response through vibration, strain, acoustic emission, and fiber-optic sensing, and separating real change from the effects of temperature and traffic.
    02 · ModelWhat Is Happening Inside?Building finite-element and multiphysics models of damage we cannot see directly, then using machine learning so they run fast enough to explore uncertainty.
    03 · DecideWhat Should We Do Next?Combining models and measurements through Bayesian updating and reliability analysis, so that inspection and maintenance choices rest on evidence.

title: About Me
text:
Structural Engineer · Researcher · Vancouver, BC
That curiosity has taken me across four countries. I studied civil engineering at Harbin Institute of Technology in China, with an exchange semester at Monash University in Australia. I then moved to UC San Diego, where I earned my M.S. and Ph.D. in structural engineering with Prof. Michael Todd.
At UC San Diego, in a research program supported by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, I studied pitting corrosion on the steel gates of navigation locks.
I simulated it with multiphysics models and machine-learning surrogates, carried its uncertainty through to a reliability analysis of a whole gate, and updated the models with laboratory measurements. As a postdoc, I turned to diagnosing damage across many similar structures.
In 2025, I joined LPI Ingenieurgesellschaft in Hannover, Germany, to look at the same question from the field: bridges in service. There I automated operational modal analysis of long-term monitoring data, studied how temperature shifts the natural frequencies of an intact and a damaged bridge, and helped interpret field measurements for bridge owners.
Teaching and mentoring have been a rewarding part of the journey, from running modal-testing labs to guiding students through their first research projects. You can read more on the Experience page, or browse the case studies.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text: Engineering Practice · LPI Ingenieurgesellschaft · 2025–2026

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
section: Two Twin Bridges, One with Broken Tendons
text:
Two Twin Bridges, One with Broken Tendons
Both prestressed-concrete bridges were built in 1966 at the same highway interchange. Later, a truck impact fractured three tendons in the southern bridge; two of its lanes were closed and its asphalt removed. Sharing a design, a site, and the weather, the twins remove many of the usual unknowns.
Each bridge carries two accelerometers sampling at 100 Hz. Temperature sensors embedded in the concrete sample at 1 Hz, so the analysis uses the temperature of the structure itself rather than of the air.



Green squares mark accelerometers; colored dots mark embedded temperature sensors. T1 is the intact bridge and T2 has documented tendon damage. Source: EWSHM 2026 presentation, slide 5, LPI.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:
Operational Modal Analysis, Automated
I automated the identification in Python with two classic methods that cross-check each other. Frequency domain decomposition finds peaks in the singular values of the measured spectra. Stochastic subspace identification fits a state-space model to the measured correlations, and a stabilization chart keeps only modes that remain stable as the model order grows.




Modal frequencies appear as peaks in frequency domain decomposition (left) and as columns of stable poles in stochastic subspace identification (right). Source: EWSHM 2026, LPI.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:
How Much Data Is Enough?
A study of block lengths from 3 to 60 minutes showed that reliable identification needs at least 10–15 minutes of data, depending on how strongly traffic excites the bridge.
Bootstrap resampling gave a 5th–95th percentile interval that reflects identification uncertainty and frequency variation within each analysis window. The intervals widened in cold weather: on the intact bridge, from 0.020 Hz at higher temperatures to 0.063 Hz at low ones.



First-mode frequency with 5th–95th percentile bootstrap bands (top) and embedded concrete temperature (bottom), from autumn 2025 through winter 2026. Source: EWSHM 2026 presentation, slide 9, LPI.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:
The Damaged Bridge Sits Lower
On average, the intact bridge vibrated at 3.52 Hz and the damaged bridge at 3.44 Hz.
That gap means more than it seems. Removing the asphalt made the damaged bridge lighter, which alone should have raised its frequency, so the stiffness loss may be larger than the offset suggests.



The intact bridge (T1, blue) has a higher mean frequency than the bridge with tendon damage (T2, orange). Source: EWSHM 2026 presentation, slide 10, LPI.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:
The Response Changes Near Freezing
A straight line fits neither bridge. Both follow a bilinear relationship with a breakpoint near 2–3 °C, below which the frequency becomes four to six times more sensitive to temperature. A similar pattern, possibly related to freezing, has been reported for the Z24 benchmark bridge.
Above the break, the damaged bridge was about 1.5 times more sensitive than its twin: −0.0089 versus −0.0058 Hz/°C. How a bridge responds to temperature, not only its frequency, may therefore carry information about its condition.




Bilinear fits for the intact bridge (T1, left) and damaged bridge (T2, right), with breakpoints at 2.54 and 2.32 °C. Point color indicates date. Source: EWSHM 2026 presentation, slide 12, LPI.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:
What It Means
Automated operational modal analysis with uncertainty bounds turns continuous vibration data into a reliable record of natural frequencies. Read against the structure’s own temperature, it shows both what temperature masks and what it may reveal. For bridges with known tendon damage, the response to temperature looks like a promising condition indicator in its own right.

title: Operational Modal Analysis and Temperature Effects on Natural Frequencies
text:

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
text: Doctoral Research · UC San Diego · 2022–2023 · USACE/ERDC

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
text:
Where the Uncertainty Comes From
Nothing about a gate in service is fixed. Water levels change with every lock operation, a gap can open where the gate should bear against the wall, and the water’s chemistry and temperature change how fast steel corrodes. I gave each of these a probability distribution.


Sources of uncertainty in the reliability analysis, after MSSP 2023

To characterize changing loads in the broader simulation study, I used USGS water levels recorded every 15 minutes at Greenup Dam. I separated the record into a trend and random fluctuations, then used a Karhunen–Loève expansion to generate water-level histories. The reliability analysis used the distributions summarized above.




The measured record is split into trend and noise, and new water-level histories are generated with the same statistics. Source: doctoral defense presentation; data from the USGS gauge at Greenup Dam.

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
section: From an Uncertain Pit to a Distribution of Crack Times
text:
From an Uncertain Pit to a Distribution of Crack Times
The surrogate from the first project carries its own uncertainty. Because it runs in seconds, I could propagate that uncertainty by Monte Carlo simulation: thousands of possible pit histories, each checked against the crack-initiation criterion. The result is not one crack-initiation time but a distribution, together with where on the pit the crack is likely to start.




Distributions of crack-initiation time and location for two loading cases, compared with the full simulation (red). Source: doctoral defense presentation; Scientific Reports 2022.

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
text:
Two Scales, Two Surrogates
Next came the whole gate. A validated, 64,919-element Abaqus model of the Greenup miter gate turns water levels and gap length into local stresses. I ran it 1,000 times and trained a global surrogate on the results; nine features captured 95% of the variation in the gate’s strain response.
A second, local surrogate turns those stresses, together with the uncertain corrosion parameters, into the probability that a crack starts within two years.




Water levels and gap length drive the gate model; its stresses and the environment drive the pit model. Source: MSSP 2023.

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
text:
Spending Simulations Where They Matter
For this reliability calculation, accurate predictions near the boundary between “safe” and “cracked” matter most. I combined importance sampling, Gaussian mixture models, and active learning to add training runs near that boundary, with a stopping rule based on a conservative bound on the probability error.
Across eleven stress conditions, the local benchmark required 101 function evaluations, compared with 674 for adaptive Kriging Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS). The benchmark used a Gaussian-process approximation of the phase-field model as its reference model.




Function evaluations in the local reliability benchmark, grouped by stress condition. Totals: 101 for the proposed method and 674 for AK-MCS. Redrawn from MSSP 2023, Table 2.

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
section: Why Risk Concentrates Low on the Gate
text:
Why Risk Concentrates Low on the Gate
Putting the pieces together gives the map at the top of this page. Risk concentrates near the bottom and below the waterline for two reasons: stresses are highest at the bottom, and steel corrodes faster in water than in air. A similar pattern appears on retired gates.

title: Uncertainty Propagation and Reliability Analysis
text:
What It Means
The analysis turns uncertain loads and corrosion parameters into a spatial forecast that can help prioritize inspections. It also makes the link between assumed conditions and predicted risk explicit. The next step was to update those corrosion parameters with measurements.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text: Postdoctoral Research · UC San Diego · 2024–2025 · USACE/ERDC

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text:
Similar, Not Identical
Two gates of the same type still differ in geometry, boundary conditions, and the water levels they hold back, and a network trained on one can mistake those differences for damage.
Domain adaptation aims for a diagnosis that is sensitive to damage but not to which structure the data came from. The labeled structure is the source; the structure to diagnose is the target, which contributes unlabeled responses during training.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
section: Two Gates on the Columbia River
text:
Two Gates on the Columbia River
I tested the idea on validated finite-element models of two downstream miter gates on the Columbia River. The Dalles was the labeled source, and Bonneville was the unlabeled target.
On both, I simulated two common kinds of damage: a gap, where the gate loses contact with the wall at the quoin block, and corrosion, as thickness loss across three zones of the gate. Water levels were sampled within each gate’s measured operating range. A sensitivity analysis then picked the strain-gauge locations that respond most to each type of damage.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
section: Learning What the Gates Have in Common
text:
Learning What the Gates Have in Common
A domain-adversarial neural network builds this in through a rivalry. A shared feature generator feeds two heads. One predicts the damage, using labels from the source gate only. The other tries to tell which gate the data came from. Training rewards features that help the first head and defeat the second, so the features keep what reveals damage and drop what reveals the structure.



The feature generator serves both a damage predictor, trained on source labels, and a domain classifier that it learns to defeat. Source: IWSHM 2025 presentation.


After training, the learned features of the two gates line up: for the same amount of damage, both gates produce similar feature values.



Learned feature values against damage level, with source and target responses following similar trends in several panels. Source: IWSHM 2025 domain-adaptation presentation, slide 10.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text:
Results on the Unlabeled Gate
On the simulated Bonneville test data, mean squared error for gap size fell from 0.069 to 0.015, a 78% reduction from the source-only baseline. Corrosion error fell from 0.221 to 0.114. Target damage labels were used to evaluate predictions after training.
A statistical check helps explain the difference. Domain adaptation assumes that damage relates to learned features similarly on both gates. Squared conditional maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD²), a measure of that mismatch, was smaller for gaps than for corrosion: 1.37 versus 12.53. Corrosion produced more structure-specific strain responses.



Predicted versus true normalized damage on Bonneville: gap length (left) and corrosion thickness loss (right). The dashed line marks exact agreement. Source: IWSHM 2025 domain-adaptation presentation, slide 9.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text:
A Different Route: Federated Learning
Domain adaptation moves knowledge from a labeled structure to an unlabeled one. Federated learning addresses a different situation: several structures each have data, but the data cannot be pooled because of ownership, privacy, or communication cost.
In a framework led by Yichao Yang, each gate trains a model locally and shares only model updates, never raw measurements. On three variants of the Greenup finite-element model, it estimated loss-of-contact damage about as accurately as centralized training. The paper received the Best Paper award at IWSHM 2025.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text:
Related Work with the Team
As a coauthor, I also contributed to work led by Yichao Zeng that translates measurements from similar gates into a common domain, then estimates damage with uncertainty through Bayesian inference and model averaging.

title: Generalized Damage Diagnosis Across Similar Structures
text:
What It Means
Together, these studies move damage diagnosis from a single, well-studied structure toward a population of similar ones, which is the situation most owners actually face. Transfer works best when damage affects both structures in a similar way, and a statistical check can show where it falls short.
